1.title: A/B Testing, Diagnosis, Optimization and Monitoring
1.text: Welcome to Module twelve: A or B Testing, Diagnosis, Optimization and Monitoring. This module covers a or b testing, diagnosis, optimization and monitoring. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. How to run A or B tests and iterate safely. A diagnosis method for prompt failures, hallucinations and model mismatch. Optimization of tokens, latency and cost without losing quality. Monitoring in production with logging and observability.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Tests a New Prompt for a Retailer's Returns Assistant
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Tests a New Prompt for a Retailer's Returns Assistant. Version B of the prompt looks better on five hand-picked examples. The client wants it live; Lumen proposes a controlled comparison first.

1.title: A/B Testing and Iteration
1.text: A or B Testing and Iteration. The figure shows this: An A or B flow: offline eval first, then a canary or split of live traffic between A and B, compare metrics with enough volume, then roll out or roll back.

1.title: A/B Testing and Iteration, continued
1.text: A or B Testing and Iteration, continued. Hypothesis. "Prompt B raises policy-correct rate by three points without raising cost". Offline first. Run both on the same dataset; reject clear losers cheaply. Online split. Randomly split live traffic (or run a shadow mode: B runs silently beside A). Change one thing. One variable per test (prompt, model, retrieval setting) so cause is clear. Metrics. Primary metric, guardrail metrics (latency, cost, safety), and a minimum sample size set in advance. Duration. Long enough for volume and weekly patterns; do not stop at the first good-looking result. Decision. Ship, iterate or revert against pre-agreed thresholds.

1.title: A/B Testing and Iteration, continued
1.text: A or B Testing and Iteration, continued. Rollout. Canary a small share, watch, then expand; keep instant rollback. Version everything: prompt, model I D, retrieval config, tool set; log the variant on every request. Compare against the current production baseline, not against nothing. Beware of noise: small samples, novelty effects and non-determinism; use repeated runs or confidence intervals for close results. Iterate in small steps; keep a change log of what helped.

1.title: Diagnosing Problems
1.text: Diagnosing Problems. The figure shows this: A diagnosis tree: integration errors, retrieval problems, prompt or context problems, model mismatch and tool problems, each with its first check.

1.title: Diagnosing Problems, continued
1.text: Diagnosing Problems, continued. H T T P errors, timeouts, truncation. Likely layer: Integration. First check: Status codes, stop reason, max tokens, retries. Confident wrong answers after data change. Likely layer: Retrieval and indexing. First check: Index freshness, retrieved chunks, embeddings. Ignores a rule; inconsistent format. Likely layer: Prompt failure. First check: Prompt version, instruction clarity, conflicting rules, examples. Invented facts or sources. Likely layer: Hallucination. First check: Were the facts in the context? Add grounding, quotes, abstain option, verification. Good on easy, poor on hard cases. Likely layer: Model mismatch. First check: Evals by difficulty; test a stronger tier or effort. Wrong tool or arguments. Likely layer: Tool design. First check: Descriptions, schemas, number of tools.

1.title: Diagnosing Problems, continued
1.text: Diagnosing Problems, continued. Slow. Likely layer: Latency. First check: Prompt length, tier, effort, retrieval depth, no caching. Cost spike. Likely layer: Tokens. First check: Cache hit rate, prompt growth, loops, model tier. Method. Reproduce with the logged request (prompt version, context, parameters). Locate the layer by checking what the model actually received (retrieved chunks, tool results) before changing the prompt. Change one variable, rerun the eval set, compare with the baseline. Add the failure to the regression set. Exam tip: Do not rewrite the prompt first. Find where the failure lives (integration, retrieval, prompt, model, tools) using logs and the exact input the model saw.

1.title: Optimizing Tokens, Latency and Cost
1.text: Optimizing Tokens, Latency and Cost. Fewer input tokens. Techniques: Cache stable prefixes; trim context; prune tool results; retrieve fewer, better chunks; compaction. Check: Cost per request, cache hit rate. Fewer output tokens. Techniques: Concise-output instructions (sentence limits), schemas, max tokens as a cap, lower effort. Check: Output tokens, truncation rate. Lower latency. Techniques: Streaming, smaller tier, caching, parallel calls, shorter prompts. Check: p ninety-five, time to first token. Lower cost. Techniques: Routing, batch for non-urgent work (fifty percent off), caching, smaller tier where evals pass. Check: Cost per successful task. Higher quality at same cost. Techniques: Better retrieval, examples, structured outputs, validation and retries. Check: Eval score.

1.title: Optimizing Tokens, Latency and Cost, continued
1.text: Optimizing Tokens, Latency and Cost, continued. Optimize cost per successful task, not cost per call: retries and wrong answers have cost. Never optimize blind: re-run the evals after each optimization; reject a saving that breaks a gated metric. Cascades (cheap first, escalate on low confidence) lower average cost and latency.

1.title: Monitoring in Production
1.text: Monitoring in Production. Reliability. Signals: Error and timeout rate, retry rate, four twenty-nines. Action: Backoff, capacity, fallbacks. Latency. Signals: p fifty, p ninety-five, time to first token. Action: Tune levers (Module ten). Cost. Signals: Tokens, cache hit rate, cost per task, spend by workspace. Action: Budget alerts, optimization. Quality. Signals: Sampled judge scores, thumbs, escalations, corrections, citation validity. Action: Regression set, prompt fixes. Safety and security. Signals: Flag rate, refusal rate, injection indicators, tool-denial events. Action: Guardrail review. Drift. Signals: Input distribution, retrieval relevance, model or prompt version changes. Action: Re-evaluate; retrain data; update chunks. Log the identifiers needed for replay (request id, trace id, prompt and model version, variant).

1.title: Monitoring in Production, continued
1.text: Monitoring in Production, continued. Use dashboards for trends and alerts on thresholds and leading indicators. Keep runbooks: who responds, how to roll back, how to fail over. Exam tip: Find the layer first (integration, retrieval, prompt, model, tools) from what the model actually received, then change one variable. Exam tip: A saving that breaks a gated quality metric is rejected: optimize cost per successful task.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. A or B: Hypothesis, offline first, one change, pre-set metrics and size, guardrails, canary, rollback. Diagnose: Reproduce; find the layer; inspect what the model saw; change one thing; add to regression. Layers: Integration, retrieval, prompt, hallucination, model mismatch, tools. Optimize: Cache, trim, concise output, route, batch, stream; cost per successful task. Rule: A saving that breaks a gated metric is rejected. Monitor: Errors, p ninety-five, cost, cache hit rate, quality sampling, safety, drift; runbooks. Log: Request id, trace id, versions, variant.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. Prompt B looks better on five hand-picked examples. What should happen before it replaces prompt A? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Controlled comparison on a dataset and live traffic avoids acting on anecdote.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. What makes an A or B test conclusion trustworthy? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Controlled design and pre-agreed thresholds protect against false wins.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A support assistant ignores a formatting rule only on long conversations. Which layer should be checked first? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Check what the model actually received before changing anything.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. An assistant invents a policy number that was never in its context. Which fix addresses the cause? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Grounding in retrieved sources, requiring citations, allowing a not-found answer and verifying numbers reduces unsupported claims.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. A system is accurate on routine cases but fails on the hardest eight percent. What does this suggest? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Evals by difficulty reveal mismatch; escalate only where needed.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Select two. Which two belong in a production monitoring plan? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Leading indicators and quality sampling catch regressions early.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. A cost-cutting change reduces tokens by thirty percent but the faithfulness metric drops below its gate. What should happen? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Optimization is accepted only if gated metrics hold.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. Which rollout approach is safest for a new model version? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A canary with instant rollback limits the harm of a faulty model version while the metrics are compared with the baseline.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. Why log the prompt version, model I D and variant on every request? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Versioned logs make behavior reproducible and let a change in quality be attributed to a specific prompt, model or variant.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Latency rose after a release while the model and traffic are unchanged. Which check is most direct? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. A longer prompt or lost cache explains latency and cost shifts.

1.title: Practice Question 11
1.text: Question eleven. An agent system's failures are hard to reproduce. Which practice helps most? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Full production tracing and checkpoints make non-deterministic multi-step runs diagnosable and resumable after a failure.

1.title: Practice Question 12
1.text: Question twelve. What is the right unit for cost optimization? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Failed or repeated attempts are part of the true cost.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all twelve answers. Question one: A. Question two: D. Question three: D. Question four: B. Question five: B. Question six: A and C. Question seven: B. Question eight: A. Question nine: D. Question ten: A. Question eleven: A. Question twelve: B. In the next module, we continue the course.
